<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases, but B did more effective work resolving the pressure points raised against it. When A's toughest challenge — "there is no principled, fraud-resistant line for 'resident'" — was pressed in the Q&A round, B answered concretely by anchoring the definition to existing municipal registers (tax, voting, school enrollment) and argued over-inclusion is low-cost; A never returned to attack this specific fix in later rounds, effectively conceding it by neglect. B also defused A's central revenue-cannibalization argument by reframing the goal as access/equity rather than pure conservation-revenue maximization, a move consistent with B's own thesis about ownership and consent. A's cleanest weapon — the revenue "dilemma" trap in A4.3–4.4 — was logically sharp but landed as a values disagreement rather than a knockout, since B had already stipulated it would trade some revenue for equity. Finally, B's closing converted A's own concession (that residents can time-shift to off-peak visits) into a decisive point: the whole dispute is about peak season, and A's fix confirms rather than refutes the exclusion the motion targets. A's closing soundbite ("a tax on the fragile thing it claims to save") was memorable but arrived without fully re-engaging the residency-definition and equity reframes B had already secured.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to A's pressure question on defining "resident" (B4.1, using existing tax/voting/school registers with generous over-inclusion) neutralized A's central "no principled line" objection, and A never rebutted that specific fix afterward.</best_rebuttal>
